newsitem.title: UK: Mark subdued on crosses despite Waigel remarks.
newsitem.headline: Mark subdued on crosses despite Waigel remarks.

text.p: The mark was subdued on its European crosses during the morning session, despite making some short-lived early gains on the dollar and sterling after remarks from German finance minister Theo Waigel.
Waigel's comment that Germany wanted a strong mark, and that the dollar and pound's strength reflected market overreaction, had limited effect on the sidelined mark crosses.
But analysts said the market remained vulnerable to German verbal intervention, and activity could increase later in the day as traders covered their shorts.

"Trade will pick up later with more short-covering in the European crosses because we haven't heard the last from Germany about the threat of intervention," said Nick Parsons, chief currency strategist at Banque Paribas in London.
The mark was quoted at 3.3776/81 French francs at 0959 GMT compared to 3.3769/72 in late Europe on Monday, and at 971.90/2.20 Italian lire versus 970.55/1.05.
"The EMS (European Monetary System) crosses is one area in the currency markets which is pretty dead," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at J.P. Morgan Europe here.
"European currencies have reached their convergence level, the level where they are discounting that they will be in EMU on January 1, 1999, at their ERM central parities."
Paribas' Parsons said the market ought to watch the German bond or bund market for the key to the mark's movements and an advance hint of Bundesbank intervention.

"The Bundesbank is very indifferent to the mark's decline, as long as bond yields are steady or falling," he said. "If yields are rising then they cannot simply stand by and watch the mark depreciate."
"The outlook for the crosses is really going to be determined by the price action of bunds."
Waigel's remarks hauled sterling down to 3.0045 marks, but it had recovered to 3.0245/55 by 1005 GMT. It finished European trading at 3.0200/10 on Monday.
